title: The second chocolate and the 21 percent
_format: 1080x1350 = 4:5. NICHT 3:4 — die Instagram-API akzeptiert beim automatischen Veroeffentlichen nur 4:5 bis 1.91:1. Bildprompts bleiben 3:4, ihre schwarze Fusszone faengt die Differenz ab.

caption.kern: A waitress offered diners a chocolate with the check. Tips went up a little. Then she offered a second one as she walked away — and tips jumped 21%. 🍫🤯
caption.detail: Strohmetz, Rind, Fisher and Lynn ran it at a restaurant in central New York in 1998: 80 dining parties, one server, four conditions, a shuffled stack of cards deciding what she did at each table. No candy: the tip averaged 18.95% of the bill. One chocolate each: 19.59%. Two chocolates each, offered at once: 21.62%. One chocolate, then — turning back at the edge of the table — one more: 22.99%. Same candy in the last two conditions. Only the way it was given changed.
caption.kontext: The authors' read: not mood and not a better impression, but reciprocity. A gift that feels extra and personal creates a pull to give something back, and the only thing on the table to give is the tip. It fits the party-size result too: the more generous she looked, the bigger the table's response. In their own back-of-envelope sum, using the second-chocolate move at every table would have added $234.73 to $1,101.02 in tips.
caption.frage: When did a small extra gesture last make you give more than you planned to?
caption.sources: Sources: Strohmetz, Rind, Fisher & Lynn — Sweetening the Till: The Use of Candy to Increase Restaurant Tipping • Journal of Applied Social Psychology 32(2): 300–309, 2002

headline: [4 RESEARCHERS] FOUND THAT
A WAITRESS EARNED [21% MORE]
BY OFFERING [CHOCOLATE]
[TWICE] AT THE TABLE
slides.alt: A waitress in a black apron holds out a small wicker basket of foil-wrapped chocolates to a seated diner in a dim Italian-American restaurant, candlelight on the table. Headline: 4 researchers found that a waitress earned 21% more by offering chocolate twice at the table.

headline: IT STARTED WITH A [BASKET]
OF [MINIATURE CHOCOLATES]
slides.body: Spring 1998. One [waitress] with five years of experience, [80 dining parties], four conditions. A shuffled stack of [index cards] told her what to do at each table: [no candy], one piece, two pieces, or one piece and then [one more].
slides.alt: A wicker basket of foil-wrapped miniature chocolates beside a fanned stack of index cards and a closed check folder on a restaurant table in warm lamplight. Headline: It started with a basket of miniature chocolates.

headline: ONE PIECE BARELY [MOVED] IT.
TWO PIECES [DID].
slides.body: No candy: tips averaged [18.95%] of the bill. One piece each: [19.59%], a nudge. Two pieces each: [21.62%] — about [14% more] than no candy at all.
slides.alt: A diner's hand lays folded bills into a check folder beside two foil-wrapped chocolates on a dark restaurant table, amber light from a table lamp. Headline: One piece barely moved it. Two pieces did.

headline: SAME [TWO PIECES].
A [DIFFERENT] WAY OF GIVING.
slides.body: She offered [one], then turned back at the table's edge and offered [one more]. Tips hit [22.99%] — about [21% more] than no candy. The amount of candy was [identical]. The [gesture] was not.
slides.alt: A waitress pauses mid-turn at the edge of a restaurant table, holding the chocolate basket out a second time to two surprised diners. Headline: Same two pieces. A different way of giving.

headline: THE [CHOCOLATE] DIDN'T DO IT.
THE [FAVOUR] DID.
slides.body: The authors point to [reciprocity], not mood: an extra, personal gesture creates a pull to [give something back] — and the only thing on the table is the tip. The more generous she looked, the [bigger the table's response].
slides.alt: Two hands meet across a restaurant table in warm amber light, one offering a foil-wrapped chocolate, the other returning a folded bill. Headline: The chocolate didn't do it. The favour did.
